messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajinder is a 79-year-old South Asian man, divorced, who has spent the last several years working shifts at a regional warehouse on the outskirts of the city — a job he took up in his late seventies partly for the income and partly, he would admit if pressed, because the noise and routine kept his mind occupied. He presented for a clinical intake with a PCL-5 score of 65, describing a longstanding constellation of symptoms that he had carried, largely in silence, for decades following his combat service.

Rajinder served as a young soldier in his early twenties, deployed into active conflict during a period of sustained and intense fighting. He witnessed the deaths of men he had trained alongside, endured artillery bombardments that left him unable to hear properly for days, and was present when a close friend was killed at close range during a ground assault. He has never spoken about the details of that assault to anyone — not to the wife he later married and eventually divorced, not to his adult children, and not to the physicians he has seen over the years for various physical complaints. He carried it the way he carried most things: quietly, and at considerable personal cost.

What brought Rajinder to the clinic now, at 79, was not a single crisis but an accumulation — a slow erosion of his ability to manage what he had always managed. He described his current state with a kind of measured exhaustion, the language of a man who has been holding something heavy for a very long time and is simply tired of holding it. His PCL-5 score of 65 reflects the full weight of that burden, placing him in the severe range, and his presentation across the intake sessions confirmed a picture of chronic, undertreated posttraumatic stress.

Rajinder's daily life at the warehouse has become, in recent months, increasingly difficult to navigate. The facility is loud — forklifts, the crack of pallet jacks, the intermittent clang of metal shelving — and he finds himself startled repeatedly across a single shift in ways that leave him shaken and embarrassed. He has not told his supervisor. He arrives early to walk the floor before others come in, orienting himself to the space in a way he could not easily explain but which feels necessary. His colleagues have noticed that he is quiet, that he does not take lunch in the break room, and that he sometimes stands very still in the middle of an aisle as though listening for something.

What Rajinder is most afraid of, he said in the third session, is that something is wrong with him in a way that cannot be fixed — that the things he has seen have made him into a person who cannot be at peace. He has come to believe this almost as a fact, the way one believes in weather. He did not use clinical language. He said, simply, that he has never felt safe since he came home, and that he is not sure he knows what safe feels like anymore.

He is hoping, cautiously, that someone can help him sleep without the images returning. He is hoping, though he did not say this directly, that it is not too late — that at 79, after more than fifty years of carrying this alone, there is still something that can be done. The divorce, years ago now, he attributes in part to his inability to be present, to his habit of leaving rooms without explanation, to a distance his former wife eventually stopped trying to cross. That loss sits alongside the original one, quieter but persistent.

He came to the clinic, he said, because his youngest daughter asked him to. He would not have come otherwise. He is not certain he deserves the help, and that uncertainty — old, familiar, and entirely his own — may prove to be the first thing worth addressing together.
